# The provenance file on Fenrir

*Catalogue entry — Fenrir. Every claim below carries its chain of custody.*

## Provenance

**1. The attestation.** **ᚠᛁᚾᚱᛁᚱ**, from the tradition's own record. On record: Snorri Sturluson, Prose Edda: Gylfaginning 34–35 (the binding of the wolf) and 51 (Ragnarök), trans. Faulkes, Poetic Edda: Vafþrúðnismál 46–47, 53 (Fenrir and the sun; Óðinn's doom), trans. Larrington, Poetic Edda: Vǫluspá (the Ragnarök stanzas; the Ironwood brood), Grímnismál 17, Lokasenna 38, Hyndluljóð 40, Cleasby–Vigfusson, An Icelandic-English Dictionary, s.v. Fenrir, Gleipnir, úlfr.

**2. The narrative record.** **The Brood of Angrboða** — Hyndluljóð says it in a line: Loki begot the wolf with Angrboða — the giantess 'herald of sorrow' who dwells in Járnviðr, the Ironwood.  Snorri names all three children of that union: the wolf Fenrir, Jǫrmungandr the world-serpent, and Hel, who is half the colour of the living and half of the dead. **Lœðingr and Drómi** — The wolf grew at a pace the gods could watch, and the prophecies grew plainer: he was fated to harm them.  So the Æsir made a strong fetter called Lœðingr and brought it to the wolf, challenging him to test his strength against it.

**3. The physical record.** Fenrir is an entirely textual monster: no cult site, votive deposit, or runic inscription invokes him, and wolves in the Scandinavian material record are read as Fenrir only by interpretation, never by name. Two famous carvings are the standing candidates. The Gosforth Cross in Cumbria (c. 900–950) carries a panel of a figure rending the jaws of a great beast — a spear in hand, one foot on the lower jaw — within what is widely read as a Ragnarök programme, and the identification with Víðarr and the wolf, argued by Bailey and most subsequent scholars, remains the standard reading, though it is an interpretation, not an inscription. Thorwald's Cross at Kirk Andreas on the Isle of Man (Manx Cross 128, tenth century) shows a figure with a bird on his shoulder and his foot in a wolf's mouth, commonly read as Óðinn devoured at Ragnarök, with his raven still upon him; the Ledberg stone (Ög 181, Sweden) has likewise been given a Ragnarök reading, more controversially. On the textual side, Vǫluspá, Vafþrúðnismál, Grímnismál, and Lokasenna survive in the Codex Regius of the Poetic Edda (GKS 2365 4to, c. 1270), Hyndluljóð in the Flateyjarbók, and Snorri's account of the binding in the Codex Regius of the Prose Edda and its sister codices of the thirteenth and fourteenth centuries.

**4. The current holding.** The temple at [/sites/fenrir/](/sites/fenrir/), classified Tier 2. Tier-2 here means one preserved truth — not less important, just singular. The temple shows it and names it.

**5. The documented resonances.** **Disaster Resilience & Recovery**, **Pet Care & Animal Industries**, **Legal, Justice & Compliance** — seats argued and weighted in the [pattern atlas](/patterns/), read through the myths in this temple's [Resonance File](/sites/fenrir/blog/resonance/).

**6. The primary sources.** [Poetic Edda](/texts/poetic-edda/), [Prose Edda](/texts/prose-edda/) — the library this file answers to, open at the [Sacred Texts collection](/texts/).

**7. The continuing record.** Fenrir is the North's most famous monster, and his afterlife runs on two tracks.  The scholarly track never stopped: the binding of the wolf was a set-piece of the Victorian Norse revival — the Kearys' Heroes of Asgard (1857) made the fetters and the pledge of Týr's hand a children's classic — and every handbook since has treated Gleipnir's six impossibles as the Edda's signature riddle-image.

- **Restored name:** Fenrir
- **ASCII form:** fenrir
- **Meaning:** "Fen-dweller (from fen + -ir)"
- **Domain of influence:** Wolf, Destruction, Binding
- **Pantheon:** Norse
